title: Matrices in place
sub: Rotate Image, Spiral Matrix, Set Matrix Zeroes: reasoning with indices and O(1) memory
cards/0/title: Rotate Image: where a cell goes
cards/0/body:
Rotate Image (LeetCode #48). A square n×n matrix (n ≤ 20); rotate it 90° clockwise in place — no second matrix.

Start with indices, not the picture. In a clockwise rotation row i becomes column n − 1 − i, and column j becomes row j: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i). Check it on a corner: the top-left (0, 0) goes to the top-right (0, n − 1). Counterclockwise is the inverse mapping: (i, j) → (n − 1 − j, i).

Brute force: res[j][n − 1 − i] = m[i][j] into a second matrix — O(n²) time and O(n²) memory. The time cannot improve — every cell has to be touched — but the memory can go.
cards/1/q: n = 4. Where does cell (1, 3) go in a 90° clockwise rotation?
cards/1/explain: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i) = (3, 4 − 1 − 1) = (3, 2). Check with the picture: the cell at the right edge of the second row moves down, to the second-from-right position of the bottom row.
cards/1/wrong/1: That is the counterclockwise rotation: (i, j) → (n − 1 − j, i) = (0, 1).
cards/1/wrong/2: That is only the transpose (i, j) → (j, i). After it the row still has to be mirrored: column 1 → 4 − 1 − 1 = 2.
cards/2/body:
The rotation splits into two simple swaps, each done in place.

1. Transpose — mirror over the main diagonal: (i, j) ↔ (j, i). Swap only the pairs above the diagonal, j > i: if you go over every j, each pair is swapped twice and ends up back where it was.
2. Mirror every row: (j, i) → (j, n − 1 − i). Together: (i, j) → (j, i) → (j, n − 1 − i) — exactly the clockwise rotation.

Counterclockwise — transpose and reverse the order of the rows. 180° — reverse the order of the rows and each row. O(n²) time, O(1) memory, n(n − 1)/2 + n·⌊n/2⌋ swaps.

Unity: this is how you rotate a tetromino in an n×n mask and the data of a room prefab — the walkability grid, the door mask. Transform rotates the prefab itself; the grid data is your code. A non-square w×h room cannot be rotated in place: the result is h×w, you need a new array, res[x, h − 1 − y] = cells[y, x].
cards/2/deep:
Rotating in fours. The second classic solution goes ring by ring: within a ring a cell moves along a cycle of four positions (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i) → (n − 1 − i, n − 1 − j) → (n − 1 − j, i), and one temporary rotates the whole four. Same O(n²) and O(1), but every cell is written once instead of twice. Transposing is easier to write without bugs, the fours are easier to explain through indices; both are accepted.

Cache. Transposing reads along a row and writes along a column. For n = 20 it does not matter; on a 4096×4096 matrix of int nearly every write is a cache miss. Blocked transposition helps: walk in squares, say 32×32, so both blocks stay in cache.

int[][] versus int[,]. LeetCode gives a jagged array: rows are separate arrays, and Array.Reverse(m[i]) reverses a whole row. That does not work for int[,] — Array.Reverse on a multidimensional array throws RankException; write a swap loop or store the grid flat (next lesson).

A rectangle in place. Transposing a non-square matrix within the same buffer is possible by following the cycles of the index permutation, but that is a separate, tricky problem. In an interview the honest answer is a new h×w array.

Tetrominoes in Unity. A piece is often stored not as a matrix but as cell offsets from a pivot: a clockwise rotation with y pointing up is (x, y) → (y, −x). The SRS rotation system adds “wall kick” tables — which shifts to try if the rotated piece hits something.
cards/3/explain: Transpose only above the diagonal: j starts at i + 1. Swap with a tuple — (m[i][j], m[j][i]) = (m[j][i], m[i][j]). Then reverse every row. Array.Reverse(m) would reverse the order of the rows — together with the transpose that is a counterclockwise rotation.
cards/4/task: Step through the rotation of a 4×4 matrix of the numbers 1..16. The rig stops twice: name the next swap.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Row 0 is transposed: (0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3) were swapped with their mirrors. Which swap starts row 1?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: j starts at i + 1 = 2: only cells above the diagonal are taken. Swapping (1, 0) ↔ (0, 1) would put 2 and 5 back where they were, and (1, 1) lies on the diagonal and maps to itself.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: The transpose is done, row 0 is [1, 5, 9, 13]. What does the first mirroring step do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Mirroring a row swaps columns a and n − 1 − a: first 0 and 3, then 1 and 2. The swap (0, 0) ↔ (3, 0) would reverse a column, i.e. the order of the rows — that gives a counterclockwise rotation.
cards/5/q: On [[1, 2], [3, 4]] this code produces [[2, 1], [4, 3]] — a mirror image, not a rotation. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: j from 0 visits every pair twice: at (0, 1) the cells swap, at (1, 0) they swap back. No transpose happened, only the row mirroring is left. It should be j = i + 1.
cards/6/body:
Spiral Matrix (#54). Return the elements of an m×n matrix (m, n ≤ 10) in clockwise spiral order, starting at the top-left corner.

No need to simulate “turns” with a visited array — keep four boundaries of the unvisited rectangle: top, bottom, left, right. One lap: the top row left to right, top++; the right column top to bottom, right--; the bottom row right to left, bottom--; the left column bottom to top, left++.

The trap: after the first two sides the rectangle may have degenerated — only one row or one column was left, and it has been walked already. So walk the bottom row only if top <= bottom, and the left column only if left <= right. Without these checks, matrices like 3×4 output elements twice.

Invariant: the unvisited cells are exactly the rectangle [top..bottom] × [left..right]. O(mn) time, memory is just the answer.
cards/7/explain: Going down follows the right column — a[i][right] — and starts from the already moved top so the corner is not read twice. The way back along the bottom row happens only if rows are left (top <= bottom), the way up the left column only if columns are left (left <= right). A finished left column moves left++.
cards/8/task: Step through the spiral over a 3×4 matrix. The rig stops twice: say what the code reads next.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: The right column was read: 8, 12, and right became 2. What does the code read next?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: The bottom row right to left, from right = 2 to left = 0: 11, 10, 9. The 12 was already read with the column — that is why right-- comes before the way back.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Skips the way back: no rows are left
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: Second lap: 6, 7 were read, top became 2 and bottom = 1. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: top = 2 > bottom = 1 — no unvisited rows remain, and the check top <= bottom keeps the code out of the way back. Without it row 1 would be read a second time, and 6 would come out twice.
cards/9/title: Set Matrix Zeroes: markers in the first row and column
cards/9/body:
Set Matrix Zeroes (#73). If a cell is 0, set its entire row and column to 0; in place. m, n ≤ 200.

The brute-force trap: zeroing immediately when you meet a 0 — the new zeroes start zeroing their own rows too, and the whole matrix ends up zero. So first mark, then fill.

Memory, step by step: a copy of the matrix — O(mn); two flag arrays rowZero[m] and colZero[n] — O(m + n); O(1) — keep the flags in the matrix itself: m[i][0] = 0 means “zero row i”, m[0][j] = 0 means “zero column j”. But the first row and first column may contain zeroes of their own — remember their fate in two bools before marking.

Order matters: 1) flags for the first row and column; 2) marking over cells [1.., 1..]; 3) zeroing cells [1.., 1..] by the markers; 4) at the very end — the first row and column by the flags. Zeroing the first row before step 3 erases the markers.
cards/10/task: Step through Set Matrix Zeroes on a 4×4 matrix with zeroes at (1, 1) and (3, 0). The rig asks twice what the code does.
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Zeroes row 1 and column 1 right away
cards/10/goal/asks/0/q: The flags are stored: firstRowZero = false, firstColZero = true. Marking reached the zero at (1, 1). What does the code write?
cards/10/goal/asks/0/explain: Markers live in the first row and first column: m[1][0] = 0 means “zero row 1”, m[0][1] = 0 means “zero column 1”. Zeroing right away is not allowed — the new zeroes would start marking on their own. There are no separate arrays: O(1) memory.
cards/10/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Leaves the first row as is: [1, 0, 3, 4]
cards/10/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Zeroes the first row: it holds a 0 marker
cards/10/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Restores m[0][1] to its old value 2
cards/10/goal/asks/1/q: The inner cells are filled. firstRowZero = false, and the first row holds the marker m[0][1] = 0. What does the code do with the first row?
cards/10/goal/asks/1/explain: The fate of the first row is decided by the flag, not by the markers in it: it had no zero of its own. The marker m[0][1] = 0 sits in the cell of the zeroed column 1 — it has to be zero anyway. There is no need, and nothing, to restore the 2 from.
cards/11/q: On [[0, 1], [1, 1]] the code zeroes the whole matrix, though the answer is [[0, 0], [0, 1]]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/11/explain: The first row is zeroed before the inner cells are filled. Its zeroes look like “zero this column” markers, and m[1][1] gets zeroed although neither row 1 nor column 1 had a zero. The first row and column go last, after the fill step.
cards/12/q: Room and piece data in Unity. What is true? Select all.
cards/12/options/0: A 6×4 room cannot be rotated 90° within the same 6×4 array — you need a 4×6 array
cards/12/options/1: A 180° rotation means reversing the order of the rows and each row
cards/12/options/2: Transposing with j from 0 rotates the matrix by 180°
cards/12/options/3: If the prefab is rotated via Transform, the door mask in the data must also be rotated by code
cards/12/options/4: Set Matrix Zeroes in place takes a single pass: zero immediately when you meet a zero
cards/12/explain: A rotated room swaps its width and height — it does not fit a buffer of the old dimensions. 180° is two mirrors: the order of the rows and each row. Transposing with j from 0 swaps every pair twice and does nothing. Transform rotates only the visuals and colliders; the grid data is your array, and your code rotates it. Zeroing immediately is not allowed: new zeroes would spread over the whole matrix.
cards/13/q: You are solving Rotate Image out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/13/items/0: Clarify: is the matrix square? clockwise? in place?
cards/13/items/1: Indices: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i), check it on a corner
cards/13/items/2: Naively: a second matrix — O(n²) memory
cards/13/items/3: Idea: transpose only above the diagonal and mirror each row
cards/13/items/6: Edge cases and variations: n = 1, counterclockwise, a rectangular matrix
cards/13/explain: The index formula comes first — both the check and the proof that transpose plus mirror is exactly the rotation rest on it. For a rectangle the honest answer is “not in place, a new h×w array”.
